# Help Your Child with Homework When You Don't Remember the Topic

> **In short:** When you've forgotten the math (or any subject) your kid is learning, ask an AI assistant to explain it in plain words you both can follow — then use that to guide them with questions, not answers.

You open the textbook and stare at a page full of words that look familiar but don't quite click. Your kid is waiting. You want to help, but you don't remember how fractions work, what a metaphor is, or why the periodic table is organized the way it is. That gap between wanting to help and knowing how is exactly where AI assistants can sit — not as a shortcut, but as your personal refresher. This guide walks you through using one (ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, or any other) to catch yourself up, so you can sit beside your kid and guide them with real confidence. One honest note up front: an AI assistant can explain the topic, but it can't see your child's face, hear their frustration, or notice when they've given up. That part is still yours.

## Before you start
- An account on any AI assistant — free plans work fine. ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, and Le Chat all handle this task well.
- A phone or computer with internet access.
- Your child's homework in front of you, even if you can't read it yet.
- About 10–15 minutes total. That's all it takes.

## Step 1 — Write down exactly what your child is stuck on
Grab a piece of paper, or open your phone's notes app to a fresh page. Write down one clear sentence about what your kid is asking for help with — not "math" but "how to find the area of a triangle." The clearer the question, the better the answer you'll get back from the assistant. You'll see a blank note waiting for input, and after a moment of thinking, you'll have a single sentence in front of you. If your child is too frustrated to explain, ask them to point at the page or read the homework question out loud. Even a half-formed sentence works — "I don't get this thing about fractions with different bottoms" — because that's plenty to start from.

💬 Example: *Find the area of a triangle when only two sides are given.*

You'll know it worked when one sentence names the topic, even if the wording is rough.

## Step 2 — Open an AI assistant and ask for a simple explanation
Open your AI assistant — the app on your phone, or the website in a browser. Paste or type the homework topic into the chat box, then add: "Explain this like I'm an adult who hasn't done it in 20 years." That tiny instruction matters — it tells the assistant to skip the jargon. You'll see a chat-style text box with a send button at the bottom (often an arrow or paper-airplane icon). After you tap send, the assistant writes back within a few seconds with a plain-language explanation. If the first reply still feels too technical, just type "Can you make it even simpler?" — every assistant will rewrite it for you.

💬 Example: *Explain like a parent who hasn't done this math in 20 years: how do you find the area of a triangle when you know the base and the height?*

You'll know it worked when the reply uses everyday words you recognize, and you're nodding along as you read.

## Step 3 — Read it out loud and explain it back to yourself
Read the assistant's answer out loud, slowly. Then close the screen and try to say the main idea in your own words, as if a friend asked you at the kitchen table. This is the most important step — it turns the assistant's words into yours. You'll see the explanation paragraph on screen, and after a moment of silence, you'll hear yourself describing it back. If a word stops you — something like "denominator" or "metaphor" — stop and ask the assistant: "Define that word in one sentence, please." Or ask for a real-life example: "What does this look like in everyday life?" A pizza slice, a road trip, a school cafeteria — analogies are how new ideas stick.

💬 Example: *Can you re-explain that with a real-life example, like measuring a slice of pizza?*

You'll know it worked when you can state the main idea out loud, in your own words, without peeking at the screen.

## Step 4 — Ask for one easy practice problem to test yourself
Before you go to your child, ask the AI for one easy practice question on the same topic, with the answer hidden until you try. Solving it yourself proves you actually understood — not just nodded along. You'll see a short problem appear on screen after a few seconds. Work it out on paper, then ask "What's the answer?" or "Did I get it right?" If the question the assistant gives you is too hard, simply say "Make it easier" or "Try a simpler one." Most assistants will keep adjusting the difficulty until the practice feels right.

💬 Example: *Give me one easy practice problem about triangle area, and only show me the answer after I try.*

You'll know it worked when you solve the practice problem correctly on your own, and the answer matches what the assistant says.

## Step 5 — Sit with your child and guide with questions, not answers
Now go back to your kid. Don't repeat what the AI told you — instead, ask questions that lead them to the answer themselves. "What does the textbook say the first step is?" "Can you draw me a picture of what the problem looks like?" "If this were a pizza, how would you figure out its size?" You'll see your child pause, then start to think out loud. They might get parts wrong — that's normal and even useful. The point is they're working the problem, not watching you solve it. When they get stuck, use the same trick: ask another small question rather than giving the answer. Their brain needs the workout, and your job is to keep them in the driver's seat.

💬 Example: *Instead of saying "It's base times height divided by two," try: "If this triangle were a slice of pizza, how would you figure out how big it is?"*

You'll know it worked when your child starts answering their own questions, even if the first few attempts are wrong.

## Step 6 — Save a one-line cheat sheet for next time
While the topic is fresh, open your notes app and write one or two sentences about what you learned — just enough to jog your memory next time. Over a school year, this short list becomes your own "parent cheat sheet," and each new homework problem takes less time to refresh on. You'll see your notes app open, and after typing for 30 seconds you'll have a single line you can return to. If you'd rather skip the notes, just bookmark the AI conversation in your browser or save it inside the app — next time the topic comes up, you can come back to the same thread.

💬 Example: *Triangle area = base × height ÷ 2. Think: pizza slice.*

You'll know it worked when you can open your notes next week and remember the gist in under five seconds.

## Common mistakes
- **Letting the AI just give your child the answer.** That's their homework, not yours. The assistant is your refresher — your kid still has to do the thinking.
- **Pretending you understand when you don't.** Kids sense this fast and trust you less. If something is still fuzzy after Step 3, stay with the AI for two more minutes until it clicks for you.
- **Stopping at the textbook answer.** Even when your child gets it right, ask "Why does that work?" or "How would you teach this to a younger kid?" That turns one right answer into real understanding.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Homework stops being a nightly stress test. You become the calm guide, not the frustrated solver, and your kid learns that confusion is just a step — not a wall.
- **For your work:** You're modeling how to learn something unfamiliar: look it up, try it, ask questions, repeat. That's a skill your kid will copy for life, in school and out of it.
- **If you're just getting started:** Don't try to use AI for every subject at once. Pick tonight's hardest problem and run through the steps for that one. Build the habit slowly, one topic at a time.

## Try it now
Tonight, pick the one homework problem your kid is most stuck on. Spend five minutes with any AI assistant understanding it yourself, using the prompts from Steps 2 and 3. Then go sit beside them and guide with a question instead of an answer. See how it feels for both of you.
